messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 43

He is 58 years old and has spent most of his adult life learning how to make sense of what others cannot bear to look at closely. As a forensic analyst, he has built a career around evidence, containment, and precision. He is married, a father, and the kind of man who usually speaks in measured sentences. Even now, he keeps a straight posture in the chair and chooses his words carefully, as if accuracy might protect him from what his body already knows.

The event that changed him happens several years ago, when a man-made disaster tears through a crowded public space where he is called to assist in the aftermath. He arrives expecting a difficult scene and instead encounters chaos on a scale that strips language away. The air is heavy with smoke, dust, and the sound of people shouting for names that are already gone. He remembers the shock of seeing ordinary objects made unrecognizable, and the helplessness of realizing that the usual rules he relies on—procedure, chain of custody, controlled observation—have no power against what has just occurred. He works because there is work to do, moving from one task to another, but something in him changes while he is there. He later says that he can still feel the moment when the scene stops looking like a case and starts feeling like a wound.

In the months that follow, he tells himself he is coping. He returns to work, keeps up appearances, and does what he has always done: he studies details, organizes facts, and avoids speaking about what he saw unless absolutely necessary. But sleep becomes unreliable. He wakes before dawn with his heart racing, already braced for something he cannot name. Sometimes he dreams in fragments—shadows, sirens, the metallic smell of the scene—and wakes convinced for a moment that he is back there. He lies still so he does not wake his wife, ashamed of how quickly his mind can drag him into the disaster again. During the day he is increasingly alert to sound: a slammed door, a backfiring car, a burst of construction noise can jolt him so sharply that he feels his chest tighten and his hands go cold.

He notices, too, that he is changing around other people. Crowds make him tense. He stops lingering in busy places and begins choosing the exit before he sits down anywhere. He avoids news coverage of explosions, fires, and public violence, but even a headline can unsettle him. He sees one image online and feels his stomach drop; for hours afterward he cannot focus and keeps checking the locks, though he knows the danger is not in his house. At work, he remains competent, but the emotional effort of staying composed takes more energy than it used to. He double-checks everything, not only because of professional habit but because uncertainty now feels intolerable. If a scene resembles the disaster in any way—smell, debris, sirens—his mind narrows, and he has to consciously bring himself back to the task at hand.

His marriage bears the strain in quiet ways. His wife notices he is more distant, less spontaneous, quicker to irritability when he is tired. He loves his family and wants to be present, but he often sits at dinner with part of his attention elsewhere, listening for sounds outside, scanning for danger that is not there. He feels guilty when he withdraws, then guilty again when he cannot explain why he needs to be alone. In private, he is not always sure whether he feels fear, anger, or sorrow most intensely. What he knows is that the disaster has left him carrying too many images and too much vigilance in a body that no longer rests easily.

Over time he becomes aware that the event is not past in the way other events are past. It returns in his sleep, in his reflexes, in the way he tracks every loud noise and every sudden change in atmosphere. He continues to function, continues to work, but with a persistent sense that part of him remains on that scene, waiting for the next blast, the next cry, the next loss he cannot prevent.
